en: Compiled by Shi Dunlun. Part One:
The *Maulī Bhūmi* Treatise, Volume One. Initial Presentation of the Discourse:
A Sixfold Analysis. First, an account of the purpose; second, a clarification of the causes. Third... [text continues]
1. Clarifying the essential tenets;
2. Manifesting the inclusion within the Tripitaka;
3. Explaining the title.
Sixth, the explanation of the main text.
First, regarding the statement of the purpose:
what is the purpose for which this treatise was composed?
As clarified in the *Śāstra*,
there are ten pairs of conditions:
first, for the sake of ensuring the long-term endurance of the Dharma and for the benefit of sentient beings.
Second, it is for the purpose of reopening what has already declined of the Noble Teaching and causing what has not yet declined to flourish even more,
as well as for leading those within the realm of sentient beings who possess the spiritual lineage out of birth and death.
First, it is for the sake of liberating those who lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*) from the miserable realms (*apāya*).
Second, it is for the sake of abandoning the views of non-existence (*asaddṛṣṭi*) and existence (*saddṛṣṭi*).

Third, it is for the sake of maturing those with the bodhisattva nature so that, relying solely upon the Great Teaching, they may develop skillful wisdom regarding the texts, meanings, practices, and fruits across all vehicles; thereby severing hindrances, attaining the fruit, and achieving the dual benefit of self and others.

Furthermore, the lack of inherent nature in the two vehicles also relies on the Great Teaching, for each gives rise to wisdom regarding the texts, meanings, practices, and fruits of their respective vehicles, thereby severing afflictions, subduing obstacles, attaining the fruits of their own vehicles, and escaping the evil realms.
Fifth, it is for the purpose of causing those who cling to false teachings and do not believe in the Mahāyāna,
as well as those who are confused by and disparage the various underlying intentions of the profound sūtras, to give rise to faith and understanding.
Sixth, it is for the purpose of gathering and benefiting those who prefer concise discourse as well as those who prefer extensive discourse.
Seventh, it is for the purpose of establishing correct treatises and refuting erroneous ones.
Eighth, it is for the purpose of revealing the four dharma-gates of the existence and non-existence of the three natures, worldly conventions, and the realization of the ultimate truth.

Ninth, it is for the purpose of opening two types of rational gateways for following and conforming to reality so that one may know that the teachings of the Two Pitakas and Three Pitakas do not contradict one another;

and for the purpose of opening four rational gateways—namely, those of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*), signlessness (*animitta*), and suchness (*tathatā*)—so that there may be distinctions in the cultivation of contemplative practice.
Tenth, it is to demonstrate the distinctions among objects so that one may know the differences in the essence, characteristics, and states of all phenomena;
and to demonstrate the distinctions among practices so that one may know the differences between the skillful means, the roots, and the fruits of the three vehicles.
Regarding such categories of intended audiences,
one should know that the various different explanations found throughout the sūtras and śāstras are all intended for this very treatise.
Second, regarding the elucidation of the causes:
according to the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra*) and other texts,
it is said that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, demonic activities arose in profusion.
The various sectarian schools arose in competition with one another,
and many became attached to views of existence.
Then, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna realized the Stage of Supreme Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).
Having collected the Mahāyāna teachings on signlessness and emptiness,
he composed the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and other works to thoroughly elucidate the essential truth and eliminate the view of existence.
The noble Āryadeva and other great masters of treatises composed the *Śataśāstra* and other works.
He extensively expounded the Great Meaning.
Consequently, sentient beings again became attached to the view of emptiness.
Nine hundred years later, there was a renunciant named Asaṅga.
In the language of Tang, he is called Wuzhuo (Asaṅga).

His birthplace was the kingdom of Ayodhyā in Central India; however, the kingdom of Gandhāra in Northern India is also [associated with him]. It is five hundred *li* west of the capital city of that kingdom.
He established a meditation center and led several hundred people, instructing them in the methods of dhyāna.
As for Wuzhuo, his spiritual rank had ascended to the first bhūmi.
Having realized the Samādhi of the Light of Dharma, he attained great supernormal powers.
He attended upon the Great Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya) and requested that he expound this treatise.
Maitreya Bodhisattva, in accordance with the capacity of Asaṅga, [taught it].
He constantly descends from the Heaven of Contentment to his meditation chamber during the night hours to recite the verses of the Five Treatises:
first, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
2. The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Treatise on the Compendium of Ascertainment); 3.
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* (Great Ornament Treatise);
4. The *Madhyāntavibhāga* (Discrimination of the Middle and the Extremes).
Regarding the Fivefold Diamond Prajñāpāramitā:
at that time, some disciples may perceive the radiance but not the marks and signs, nor hear the instructions;
others may perceive the marks and signs but not hear the teachings.
There may have been those who saw or heard [these teachings],
yet because the generations have long since passed and their names have vanished,
there remain only Asaṅga and the devas who, through their mutual realization, were moved by the transformation of Maitreya and partook of his various instructions.

In this treatise, there is no principle that is not exhausted, no phenomenon that is not fully explored, no passage that is not explained, no meaning that is not elucidated, no doubt that is not dispelled, no attachment that is not shattered, no practice that is not complete, and no fruit that is not realized.
Were it not for high-minded gentlemen of profound discernment, who else could truly join in the chanting and responding here?
Dharma Master Xuanzang, possessing a capacity that transcends the world, laments the obstruction of the current as it flows back toward its source.
Thus, he was able to depart from Yumen and journey afar to Ganashala to devote himself to the Way.
He eventually arrived at Nālandā Monastery in the kingdom of Magadha in Central India,
where he met the Great Tripitaka Master Śīlabhadra.
Upon first hearing the principles and meanings of this treatise, my comprehension was as if pouring from one vessel into another.
Although I had traveled through various countries and thoroughly mastered the subtleties of numerous texts,
it was specifically upon studying the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena) that I found particular inspiration in this work.
Subsequently, he returned to the capital and,
by imperial decree, began the translation of this treatise at Hongfu Monastery on the fifteenth day of the fifth month of the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month of the twenty-second year, I ceased writing and concluded my session.
This treatise consists of forty thousand ślokas in its Sanskrit original;
each śloka contains thirty-two syllables.
It was translated in one hundred fascicles.
Since the Dharma first arrived in the East, many years have passed;
although the name of the *Seventeen Stages Treatise* (*Saptadaśabhūmi-śāstra*) had been heard, [it remained untranslated].
Yet it is not known what these seventeen are.
The *Bhūmivastu* and the *Śīlasaṃvara* constitute only one stage (*bhūmi*) of the Bodhisattva;
the *Viniscayasamgrahaṇī* is the initial section of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
In other parts of China, these have not yet existed; the *Śīlasamvara-sūtra* was translated by Guṇavarman, and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* was translated by Dharmakṣema.
It is traditionally said that during the time of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty...
In the fourth year of the Taicheng era of the True Dharma (Zhendi), the year being Gengwu, in the tenth month,
[the Master] went to the residence of Lu Yuanzhe, the Magistrate of Fuchun,
to translate the *Seventeen Stages Treatise* (*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*) for twenty virtuous monks, including Zheqiong and others.
I originally obtained only five fascicles;
now, for the first time, the sections are complete,
and both the text and its meaning are perfectly clear and luminous.
Vast and expansive, its brilliance shines brightly through the layers of concealment;
resonant and harmonious, its sound fills the universe with the sound of the voiceless.
This may be called straightening the hooves and harnessing the carriage upon the dark path.
This opens up the profound mystery within the empty chamber.
Third, regarding the clarification of the essential tenets:
the *Śāstra* (Treatise) states in its latter section:
Furthermore, the seventeen stages (saptadaśa-bhūmi) comprehensively encompass all the textual and doctrinal content almost entirely;
the final four sections are all intended to explain the essential textual and doctrinal points within those seventeen stages.
Therefore, nothing is separated from the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
For this reason, this treatise takes the seventeen levels (*bhūmi*) as its essential core.
Fourth, regarding the inclusion within the Piṭakas:
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states in the second part:
"Although it comprehensively clarifies the objects and so forth of all vehicles,
the speaker [proceeds] to resolve and determine the nature and characteristics of all phenomena through questions and answers."
The intention is that all beings may become skillful Bodhisattvas, attain the fruit of Buddhahood, and bring about infinite benefit and happiness;
therefore, this treatise belongs to the Abhidharma of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
In order to cause bodhisattvas to attain superior wisdom,
the fifth section explains the title:

it is titled *The Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, specifically the first part, "The Stage Corresponding to the Five Collections of Consciousness" (*Pañcavijñānakāya-saṃprayukta-bhūmi*) within the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
The commentary states:
"The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* is the general title for the entire work as a whole."
In its original Indian pronunciation, it is called *yoga*.
During the Tang dynasty, there was no definitive name for it;
just as the term *gautama* encompasses nine meanings and cannot be properly rendered by a single name, so too is this case.
Therefore, the original pronunciation is retained.
Now, establishing the meaning according to the intent of the *Yogācāra* is likewise so.
For the time being, we shall adopt one sense and call it "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*).
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) provides a general definition of its essence,
stating: "All dharmas— namely, the objects, practices, and fruits of all vehicles— are called yoga,
because they all possess the sense of being associated with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)."
The intention here is to state that all objects, practices, and fruits of the three vehicles are termed "yoga.
This is because both the objects and the practices/fruits, as well as the practices and the fruit-dharmas, possess the sense of being conjoined with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
The essence of skillful means (upāyakauśalya) is,
when based on the post-attainment wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) of the ten perfections,
the manifestation of both internal and external skillfulness.
Its essential nature consists solely of the discernment (*prajñā*) among the specific objects of cognition (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*).
Now, this skillfulness, based on the explanation of the following passage, takes both attention (*manasikāra*) and discernment as its nature.
If one attends to this and further realizes and penetrates this, [it is skillful].
Therefore, the object, the practice, and the fruit do not contradict one another;
for when the mind is focused with thorough penetration, they are all in accord.
According to the *Vyākhyāyukti*, each of these three—object, practice, and fruit—is explained in three distinct ways.
Within the objective sphere, there is both the general and the particular.
Regarding the general, it is said: "All objective spheres possess the nature of being non-erroneous and the nature of being non-contradictory."
It is capable of conforming to the nature [of reality],
tending toward the ultimate nature,
and is in accord with the correct principles, teachings, practices, and fruits.
Therefore, it is called "yoga" (union).
This is because, respectively, the four objects correspond with and do not contradict principle, teaching, practice, and fruit.
That which is the objective referent of all mental states is termed an "object."
That which is realized by various forms of knowledge is termed "principle" (*nyāya*).
Principle is profound while its object is shallow;
the object apprehended by the mind possesses the nature of being non-erroneous.
That which is grasped as existing— whether conditioned or unconditioned—
is not inconsistent with the principle realized by wisdom;
whereas the existence or non-existence of a self and phenomena is [inconsistent with it].
It is true that the nature of objects is inverted; however,
they are not actually so,
because such a view does not accord with correct reasoning.
The non-erroneous nature of the object accords with principle;
the object does not contradict the teachings;
it is able to accord with practice and lead toward the ultimate fruit.
The same may be understood for the others.
Alternatively, these four are the fourfold Two Truths,
because these four objects correspond respectively with principle, teaching, practice, and fruit.
In the separate explanation of the objects, five scriptural authorities are cited to establish six types of objects.
First, some explain that the four principles— such as dependence (*apekṣā*) and so forth—
are called "yoga," because these four comprehensively encompass all correct principles.
Some say that among the twenty-four factors dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), one is named yoga because cause and effect correspond to one another.

Both of these [meanings] are explained extensively in various places, such as the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, where it is stated that the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) in both the defiled and the pure is called yoga.
Because it is most excellent for removing what is contrary to the pledge and conforming to what is in accord with it—
as stated in the *Brahmaparipṛcchā-sūtra* and other texts—
it is taught three times that suchness (*tathatā*) is called yoga.
It is the most supreme among principles,
because it is endowed with all virtues;
as stated in the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra.
The fourth [position] states that from one dharma up to a hundred dharmas, all are termed *yoga*,
because although the dharma-gates differ, their meaning is not contradictory;
as stated in the *Mahārthavargīya-sūtra*.
The fivefold teaching of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), and the truths (satya) is all termed yoga,
because it encompasses all objects of cognition and accords with the capacities of sentient beings,
as stated in the *Vastu-viśeṣa-sūtra*.
The commentary states:
Herein, the first three [of the six objects] correspond respectively to the dependent, the imagined, and the perfected natures.
These six objects all conform to the four kinds of phenomena—such as being non-erroneous and so forth—because they possess those four natures.
Within the practice of yoga, there are also general and specific aspects.
Generally stated:
it means that all practices are mutually concordant.
Because it accords with correct reasoning,
because it conforms to the authentic teaching,
and because it leads toward the correct fruit.
This is called Yoga.
There are seventeen distinct [sections],
as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The correct cultivation of all practices is called yoga,
because it comprehensively subsumes all corresponding activities;
as stated in the *Dvayamāsadīpa-sūtra*.
The cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is called yoga,
because it is the most excellent among all things conducive to the fruit.
This is stated in the *Tri-svabhāva-ṣaḍ-āyatana-sūtra*.
The path of the equal operation of śamatha and vipaśyanā is called yoga,
because it is the master of all practices;
thus it is stated in the Sāgara-mati-sūtra.
Cultivating samādhi is called yoga,
because the practice of mental abiding and the arousal of activity are most powerful therein;
this is stated in the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Fivefold Manifestation Treatise) and other texts.
The four factors of faith, aspiration, skillful means, and diligence are called yoga,
because these four give rise to all practices.
This concludes the sixth stage, the Stage Consisting of Hearing.
The nine paths, including the mundane and supramundane, are separately identified as *yoga*,
because they are distinguished by their superior status in the stages of realizing the principle and eliminating delusion.
Seventh is the stage consisting of that which is cultivated through practice (*bhāvanā-mayī-bhūmi*).
The general explanation of cultivating the various paths of counteraction is termed *yoga*,
because it provides a summary of cultivation for those who prefer brevity;
this is stated in eight locations.
The non-erroneous knowledge encompassed by the various stages (*bhūmi*) is called yoga,
because it is supreme among practices.
Thus it is stated in nine places.
Skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) or skillful means alone is termed *yoga*,
because it excels in the application of mental attention (*manasikāra*), wisdom (*jñāna*),
and the initiation of practice; or because it excels in initiating the first awakening of realization.
The *Daśaguṇa-tattva-sūtra* states that the contemplation of dependent origination is called yoga,
for it is the most essential means for transcending birth and death.
The *Ekadaśāṅgasamyakpratipadāsūtra* states that the Noble Eightfold Path, beginning with right view,
is called yoga because it is the most excellent means for proceeding toward the city of Nirvāṇa.
The *Dvādaśadharmaka-sūtra* states that the cultivation of ethical discipline and so forth is called yoga, because the trainings in ethical discipline,
concentration, and wisdom are preeminent among the causes.
The *Thirteen Great Meanings Sūtra* states that all distinctions in the stages of cultivating mundane and supramundane practices are termed yoga,
because they accord with and conform to the levels of correct practice.
The above explains the common practice of the three vehicles;
the following four pertain exclusively to the Mahāyāna.
This is stated in the *Caturdaśaprajñāpāramitāsūtra*.
The mental attention that contemplates emptiness is called yoga,
for it is the most excellent for initiating the great practice.
Fifteenth, that same sutra further states that crossing over excellence is called yoga.
Because this guides one toward the practice of the Mahāyāna, it is superior;
as stated in other sources,
the non-conceptual concentration subsumed within this perfection of wisdom is called yoga.
Because it is able to give rise to all supreme virtues.
Seventeenth, another passage further states:
"The simultaneous and equal operation of a bodhisattva’s wisdom and compassion is called yoga."
Because it is able to realize the great nirvana of non-abiding,
there are also general and specific [explanations] within the *Phala-yoga* (Yoga of the Fruit).
Generally, it says:
This means that all fruits are mutually concordant,
accord with correct reasoning,
and conform to the authentic teaching.
It is called "yoga" because it accords with the primary cause.
In the detailed explanation, seven scriptural authorities are cited.
The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states: "Power (*bala*),
fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*), and the unshared Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are called yoga because they subdue all Māras,
refute heterodox arguments, and excel over other vehicles."
The *Dvayaviśeṣa-sūtra* states:
"The Buddha’s nirvana without abiding is called yoga,
because it does not abide anywhere throughout the limits of the future."

The *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the Buddha-stage are called "yoga," because they are eternally inexhaustible in benefiting oneself and others.

Fourth, the *Yogācārabhūmi-sūtra* explains that all the qualities of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) are termed "yoga," because they extend to the limit of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) without interruption or exhaustion.
The *Pañcavyavasthāna-triyānaguṇa-sūtra* states:
"The fruits and virtues of the three vehicles are called yoga,
because they all correspond with correct principle (*nyāya*)."
The *Ṣaṭpāramitāsaṃcayagāthā-śāstra* states:
"The three bodies and the three virtues are all yoga,
because all resultant virtues are inseparable."
The *Saptasamuccayārthaśāstra* states:
"The collection of all conditioned and unconditioned merits subsumed within the state of fruition is yoga,
because it is the stage of ultimate integration through meditative attainment (*samāpatti*)."
This teaching on the object, the practice, and the fruit is called yoga.
Regarding the word "etc. (ādi) mentioned earlier in the initial heading, the commentary further states:
This noble teaching is also called yoga,
because it accords with correct reasoning and conforms to correct practice.
Because it leads to the fruition of correctness,
this passage is easily understood;
since it is included within the stage of entering the principle (*nyāma*), it is not explained further.
There is an interpretation that the term "yoga" specifically refers to the contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā*) of the three vehicles.
This is because by repeatedly cultivating these practices in accordance with reason and proceeding in conformity with them, one attains superior fruits;
furthermore, the objects, the fruits, and the sacred teachings are the domains of yoga.
Because it is the fruit of yoga and because it expresses yoga,
it is also called "yoga."
However, when examining the interpretations from ancient and modern times across both preceding and succeeding generations, they may be consolidated into four categories:
first, taking only the practice; second, taking the object, the practice, and the fruit; third, [taking the object and the practice]; and fourth, [taking the fruit].
Third, taking both [the treatise and] the teaching together;
fourth, these three together,
as explained in the commentary.
The preceding section has explained the first topic,
the second principle,
and the third practice.
Fourth, the fruits.
Fifth, having perfected the attainment of the fruits, one benefits sentient beings and rescues all things, with medicine and disease corresponding to one another;
these, taken together from beginning to end, comprise four types.
There is an interpretation:
it is called "correspondence" (saṃprayoga) because of four meanings herein.
First, the profound convergence of teaching and principle.
Second, the fruits of practice correspond in profound harmony.
Third, the spheres of wisdom coincide with perfect accord.
Fourth, emptiness and existence are non-dual.
If teaching does not accord with principle, there will be discordance and it will be difficult to attain progress.
If practice does not correspond to the fruit, the merit of cultivation and construction will be in vain.
If wisdom does not harmonize with the object, the function of illuminating things will be biased.
There is an emotional attachment that does not immediately realize emptiness, which leads to its abandonment;
in Sanskrit this is called *ācārya*,
which here means "teacher."
He possesses the merit of harmonizing and transforming others;
he crafts things according to their capacities—
this is the beautiful title bestowed upon him by his followers.
The commentary explains:
Practitioners of the three vehicles, through the sequential cultivation of hearing, reflection, and so forth,
bring such yoga to fulfillment according to their respective degrees.
They are called "Yogācāras" because they successively discipline and transform all sentient beings.
Alternatively, the Tathāgatas have realized the perfection of yoga;
accordingly, they maintain this yoga to discipline and transform all noble disciples, causing them to cultivate correct practice in successive stages.
Therefore, they are called *yogācāras*.
In Sanskrit, this is *bhūmi*;
here it is translated as "ground" (*di*).
This establishes the meaning of abiding and maintaining [the Dharma].
Beginning from the five consciousnesses and extending to the state of nirvana without remainder,
it encompasses all causes and effects of both mundane and sagely beings, leaving nothing unprepared.
All [dharmas] possess the capacity to generate, sustain, and maintain;
because they resemble the earth, it is so called.
The *Śāstra* explains:
"Ground" (bhūmi) refers to the objective sphere (viṣaya),
the basis, the domain of activity, or the sense of being encompassed;
it is the objective sphere of activity for the yogācāra.
Therefore it is called "ground" (*bhūmi*).
It is like the ground for a dragon-horse;
because one travels only within this and does not go outside of it.
Alternatively, because yogins increase their own dharmas based on this locus, it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*),
like a field for sowing crops. Or,
the wisdom subsumed within the ground of the yogin manifests based upon this and increases based upon this.
Therefore it is called "ground" (*bhūmi*),
like a ground of precious jewels;
or, it is so named because yogis practice within it and experience their own Dharma therein.
Therefore, it is called "ground" (*bhūmi*),
like the ground of a bull-king.
Alternatively, the Tathāgatas are called "yoga-masters."
Because the wisdom of equality and so forth proceed within the yoga of non-abiding nirvāṇa, which is the realm of all non-conceptual proliferation,
and because they are subsumed therein, it is called a "ground" (bhūmi).
Alternatively, because the seventeen stages encompass all practitioners of yoga (yogācāra),
they are like the domain of a king;
therefore, they are called the "Stages of the Practitioners of Yoga" (Yogācārabhūmi).
The commentary states:
Regarding its objects and what they encompass, there is only one interpretation for each.
Regarding the two types—reliance and practice—there are two interpretations for each.
This is the combined sixth section of the commentary.
In Sanskrit it is called śāstravyākhyāna;
here it is translated as "Explanatory Treatise" (Lunshi). The treatise states:
It is called a *śāstra* (treatise) because it provides definitive analysis through questions and answers regarding the nature and characteristics of all phenomena.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"It is called a *śāstra* because it instructs students."
In that case, "the teacher of yoga" (yogācārya) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound,
analyzed as "the teacher who possesses yoga."
The "stage of the yoga practitioner" (yogācāryabhūmi) is also analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound:
yoga itself is the stage.
The two entities are not distinct:
the "ground" (bhūmi) is that which is explained,
while the "treatise" (śāstra) is that which explains it.
The treatise on the *Yogācārabhūmi* is also analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound; thus,
they are combined to form the title *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
There are three explanations.
The *Śāstra* asks:
"Since this treatise consists of five parts..."
Why is it called only the *Yogācārabhūmi*?
There are three explanations.
Regarding the first explanation:
The first part is called "ground" (bhūmi),
whereas the latter four are not so named; therefore,
since the name is established based on the first part, there is no error.
Second explanation:
All phenomena (*dharmas*) are the stages of the yoga practitioner (*yogācārabhūmi*),
because the yoga practitioner takes all phenomena as their basis and objective conditions (*ālambana*).
In this context, for the sake of brevity, seventeen [categories] are explained;
through these three interpretations,
the seventeen stages fully encompass all textual and thematic meanings with complete conciseness.
The latter four quarters all serve to explain the essential textual meanings within the *Seventeen Grounds* (*Saptadaśabhūmi*);
therefore, they likewise do not depart from this [work].
The final two [quarters] explain that all five are termed "grounds" (*bhūmi*).
If this were merely called the "Yogic Stage," it would not be known whose stage it is; therefore,
the name of the Master is specified.
It mentions only "the stages of the masters" (*ācāryabhūmi*) without mentioning "yoga," leaving it unclear what kind of master’s stage this refers to.
For this reason, it is collectively termed the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
As for the statement that "the Yogācāra master does not mention the stage," it is not intended merely to clarify the provisional nature of the Yogācāra master; rather,
it is intended to explain the dharmas upon which that master relies, so that one may practice in accordance with them to become such a master and realize that stage.
The phrase "within the *Maulī Bhūmi*" (Local Division) is a specific designation for this section.
In the Sanskrit language, it is called *tala*.
This is called the "Root.
These various great structural divisions clarify the stages (*bhūmi*).
Since the stages do not illuminate themselves, they are divided into five sections to elucidate their essential meaning.
Although the five divisions are distinct, they ultimately converge upon the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Therefore, the first division is named "The Basic Stages" (*Maulī Bhūmi*),
as explained previously.
In the Sanskrit language it is called *vargī*;
here it is translated as "division" (*fenzhong*).
"Division" refers to a distinct branch or category.
Although this treatise consists of a hundred fascicles,
it distinguishes its tenets according to the stages (bhūmi).
Thus, the tenets need not be elaborated further.
The branches are separately opened into five;

Question: How does this differ from what was stated previously? What is the distinction between the aspects (ākāra)?
Answer: The previous [explanation] distinguished the aspects in relation to their objects.
This passage distinguishes the modes of activity (*ākāra*) by way of practice and understanding.
Regarding that which "has an object" (*sālambana*), a question is asked:
what is the difference between this and having the same object (*ekālambana*)?
Answer: First, the similarities and differences are clarified.
This clarifies that [the mind] must rely [on an object].
There is an interpretation [to this effect].
Previously, identity was established by way of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
now, the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is established by way of the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Regarding that which possesses a basis (*sāśraya*):
This is because it necessarily relies upon three bases.
From this point downward, the text clarifies its functions; within this section, there are two parts.
First, it clarifies its function in relation to the five consciousnesses.
The subsequent section clarifies the non-common karma.
The initial passage contains seven points;
the first is the discernment of its own object.
Regarding the two, specifically and generally characterized phenomena:
when the consciousness of direct perception takes the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena as its object,
if this cognition were to know the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of those phenomena, [it would contradict its nature].
Therefore, the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) realizes the suchness of its own specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).

Question: If this is so, why is it stated among the Three Seals of the Dharma that the two kinds of emptiness constitute the common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) of all phenomena? Answer: [The explanation follows: *Note: The original text ends with "解云" (the explanation says), indicating that a further explanation was intended but not provided in the source fragment.*
With what is it identical?
If one asserts that True Suchness (tathatā) possesses a distinct characteristic of being free from marks that differs from phenomena,
then one is asserting that True Suchness is termed its own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
This very principle of *tathatā* (suchness), which governs all categories of phenomena, is nonetheless a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
It pertains to the three periods of time and the four types of continuity and discontinuity.
Fifth, it initiates karma through two types of transformation;
sixth, it attracts maturation (*vipāka*);
and seventh, within the preliminary stage (*pūrvaprayoga*), it gives rise to the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) by means of attention (*manasikāra*).

Furthermore, within the states of defilement and purity, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the three natures acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) to induce the various consciousnesses in their subsequent state of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Regarding this, Master Ki judges that the sixth consciousness possesses all seven of these [causal functions].
Regarding the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, with the exception of those [factors] that initiate karma and summon maturation, there are five remaining parts.
Master Jing said:
"The first and the last three are common to the five consciousnesses; their karma is not uncommon."
The four intermediate karmas can be performed by the mental consciousness alone.
According to this master, the seventh category is divided into two;
therefore, it is said that "the latter three" [are so designated].
Now, the judgment is as follows:
in the first stage of practice, all eight consciousnesses are present;
in the second stage, the seventh and third consciousnesses are fully present.
The remaining seven consciousnesses exist partially;
the fourth [consciousness], karma, and the six consciousnesses exist pervasively;
the seventh and eighth exist partially.
Regarding the fifth [consciousness], the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is fully present;
the five sensory consciousnesses are partially present;
and it is absent within the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses].
Regarding the sixth karma, it is present across all six consciousnesses,
but absent within the seventh and eighth;
this is based on their coarse characteristics.
If one examines this in detail, it can be understood through careful reflection.
Below, in the section clarifying the unique functions of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
fifteen categories are first set forth and enumerated.
The subsequent analysis by way of categories concerns whose mind possesses the six factors that are not shared:

namely, those who have become detached from desire, those who have regressed from detachment, those who have severed their roots of goodness, those who have reconnected them, those who are being reborn, and those who are dying.
In the Mahāyāna, there are not only fifteen;
there are further factors such as regret (*kaukṛtya*), sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and so forth.
Therefore, the treatise employs the term "and so forth" (*ādi*).
Within the discrimination of objects of focus,
there is the discrimination of signs;
this is according to the Abhidharma.
Among the three types of discrimination, two— namely, intrinsic-nature discrimination and recollective discrimination—
are included [within the five consciousnesses], because the five consciousnesses lack an intrinsic nature as a substantial entity.
Among the seven types of discrimination, spontaneous discrimination is precisely the five consciousnesses.
In this treatise, intrinsic discrimination (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) is spontaneous;
therefore, it is said to possess a characteristic (*sanimitta*).
This is because it consists solely of recollection (*anusmaraṇa*) regarding an object previously experienced.
This differs from that treatise regarding its breadth and narrowness;
alternatively, it may be identical to both gates of the Abhidharma.
The meaning previously apprehended is comprised within the self-nature and the recollective conceptualization.

Because in the state of the resultant mind (*niṣyanda-citta*), there is conceptualization with signs (*sanimitta-vikalpa*) that takes as its object the previously perceived sphere by means of the initial, sudden mind (*ābhoga-citta*).
Master Ki judged this, saying:
"It is not as explained before."
Regarding the paths of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*):
"deportment" refers to manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*),
while the substance of the "paths" consists of the four [non-manifest] elements.
Because the four objects [of the senses] are the basis for those [actions], they are called the "modes of deportment" (*airyāpathika*).
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the modes of deportment have the four objects as their intrinsic nature.
The path is that which gives rise to those [wholesome] states of mind and serves as their support;
thus, the mind is said to be the path.
The same applies to the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).
However, because there is a distinction between the five objects and the four objects of sensory experience,
among these, deportment (*iryāpatha*) is mostly established upon the road,
while craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) is mostly established in a location.
Therefore, "place" (sthāna) and "path" (mārga) are synonymous;
both manifest the same meaning.
The seventh [consciousness], *vikalpa* (discrimination), takes vitarka and vicāra, or the five, seven, or eight consciousnesses, as its substance.
Spontaneous discrimination consists of the five, six, and seven consciousnesses.
The seventh [consciousness] is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), though it may also be associated with the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
This is explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Question: According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, spontaneous conceptualization (*svarasavāhin vikalpa*) also extends to the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*).
Why, then, is it explained here in this treatise within the context of non-common karma (*asādhāraṇakarma*)?
Answer: According to the interpretation based on the Tripiṭaka, the Abhidharma is the correct authority.
Nevertheless, this treatise introduces seven types of discrimination; therefore, it has come to be presented here.
Spontaneous conceptualization (*svarasavāhin-vikalpa*) is in fact not unique [to the mental consciousness].
Question: If there is no self-nature conceptualization (*svabhāvavikalpa*) within the five sensory consciousnesses, how then is the statement in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* to be reconciled?
That treatise refutes the Saṃmitīya position that the physical heart is the sense faculty of mind (*manas*), stating:
"If the mental consciousness were to take the physical heart as its sense faculty,
then at all times there would be no discerning or recollective conceptualization, and only innate conceptualization would exist."
Regarding the phrase "because it is like the five consciousnesses," the Tripiṭaka Master explains:
that school admits that within the five consciousnesses there is intrinsic discrimination (*svabhāva-vikalpa*).
The Master of the Treatise enters into the refutation of other schools;
he does not refute [the opponent] by means of Mahāyāna doctrine.
As for "that which is examined as the object":
Master Bei says:
Because one repeatedly conditions the preceding object and deliberates upon those conditions,
the meaning of the four inversions is as explained below in the eighth [section].
Regarding "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*),
Master Jing states:
"To know that the fruits of the three realms— superior, middling, and inferior— reside within their causes is called knowledge of the stability of phenomena."
This is conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
What follows below is called supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*);
these are precisely the two types of wisdom.
Master Ki said:
"The knowledge of the abiding of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna) is conventional knowledge (yathā-vad-jñāna);
supramundane knowledge is ultimate knowledge (yathā-bhūta-jñāna)."
Master Bei said:
"Because this wisdom arises based on the teachings of the Dharma, it is called 'wisdom of the abiding of phenomena' (dharmasthitijñāna).
This is subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna)."
Regarding "the intoxicated," Master Ji says:
"This has four conditions."
Its essence consists of lethargy, agitation, heedlessness, forgetfulness, distraction, greed, hatred, and so forth;
alternatively, its nature is that of the mind and mental factors occurring simultaneously.
According to one interpretation, it pervades the five sensory consciousnesses.
Because the mind is predominant, it is explained specifically [as such].
Master Jing says there are five conditions;
for madness, there are five conditions.
The *Abhidharmakośa*, chapter fifteen, states:
"Because it relies upon discordant primary elements (*mahābhūta*), the mind consequently loses mindfulness (*smṛti*);
therefore, one knows that its essence consists of false mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*)."
Alternatively, it has as its nature both mind and mental factors arising simultaneously;
this exists in all five destinies of the desire realm, excluding the Northern Continent,
because the people of the Northern Continent are free from affliction.
Because the various devas exist,
the Buddha exists in the Hinayana;
it is not so in the Mahayana.
The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are likewise non-existent.
*Marmāṇi* refers to the "vital points" of death;
they are also called the "joints of death."
Some say there are sixty-four locations,
or perhaps one hundred and twenty.
There are seven conditions for dreams.
Regarding the fourth, mental attention to the aspect of darkness (*tamas-lakṣaṇa*):
Master Jing says that not understanding the phenomena (*dharma*) is called the aspect of darkness.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation: because one delights in contemplating the Dharma before falling asleep, it results in a dream;
alternatively, because one contemplates the appearance of darkness with eyes closed, it leads to sleep and dreaming.
Seventh, it is induced by others.
There are four ways of being induced by others.
Question: What is the essential nature of a dream?
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* presents six explanations;
the *pūrvapakṣa* (the critical school) takes the mind and mental factors as its essence to be correct.
Now, in the Mahāyāna as well, it takes the mind and mental factors associated with sleep (*middha*) as its essence.
Furthermore, as stated in the thirty-seventh fascicle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*:
Question: Are the wholesome dharmas that arise during sleep or dreams acquired through application (*prayoga-labdha*) or acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*)?
Answer: They are exclusively acquired by birth.
Because it is dull and subtle,
other masters say that it is also [a result of] preparatory wholesome action.
Because it also involves the discernment of both words and meanings,
the Mahāyāna here also includes the wholesome state of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśala*),
as stated in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-sūtra*.
In the Buddha-land of Wondrous Consciousness above, sentient beings receive transformation and only attain awakening within a dream.
That Buddha preaches the Dharma to the spiritual consciousnesses of all sentient beings while they are asleep.
The consciousnesses of those being transformed attain the four fruits of realization up to that of a Pratyekabuddha according to their respective capacities;
they also enter parinirvāṇa while sitting cross-legged even within dreams.

From such passages as "The bodhisattva’s reception of the prediction [of enlightenment] up until his attainment of Buddhahood all occur within a dream," it is known that this also extends to preparatory wholesome states (*prayoga-kuśala*).
There are three conditions for awakening from sleep.
Regarding the statement that "one who increases sleep cannot overcome that extreme exhaustion":

because one has slept for a long time, one cannot overcome the exhaustion and must wake up again; furthermore, regarding the statement "because one makes a vow to sleep when there is work to be done":
[it means] one intends to sleep after completing the task.
During the initial stage of sleep, such as when striking the five watches of the night, one must awaken to perform prostrations to the Buddha and so forth;
in all such cases, the nature [of these states] consists of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Because they arise from four conditions, torpor (*styāna*) occurs in both states with and without consciousness.
It also has the mind and mental factors as its nature,
for it is induced by that oppressive contact which draws forth mental distress.
Awakening likewise has the mind and mental factors of that particular state as its essence.
Regarding the four conditions for the initiation of karma,
the first three correspond respectively to the three types of volition (cetanā).
That is to say: deliberation, determination, and initiation.
According to the Hīnayāna, the first two correspond to the afflictions abandoned through both seeing and cultivation, while the third is abandoned solely through cultivation.
Now, based on the Mahāyāna, one generates karma that results in a collective retribution.
The first two [categories] pertain to both the paths of seeing and cultivation,
while the third consists exclusively of the afflictions of the path of seeing.
If one generates wholesome volitions that result in a general retribution, all three types of volition are wholesome.
Even when they directly induce afflictions, these are not the non-associated ignorance (*asamprayukta-avidyā*) and so forth that are abandoned through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
For this reason, the Sūtra says:
Because the noble ones have eternally abandoned the non-common ignorance that accompanies their cognitions, they do not create new karma.
The Abhidharma also states:
"Ignorance regarding the ultimate truth gives rise to meritorious and immovable karma."
The non-meritorious karma produced by worldly ignorance is entirely abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
If one produces karma that results in distinct retribution, the third volition (*cetanā*) therein also pertains to the afflictions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Regarding the phrase "next, conforming to the function," this refers to the karmic winds that arise in each moment.
These winds conform to the third function, giving rise to volition regarding karma.
Since they simultaneously induce [the activity of] body and speech,
the *Śataśāstra* (Hundred-Verse Treatise) refuting the Vaiśeṣika school states:
"According to you, the self is immobile."
"How can it initiate karma?
He counters with this objection:
"Your mind and mental factors are likewise a single, non-moving phenomenon."
"How can karma be produced?
Deva replied:
"Although the mind is not in motion, first, through mental vitarka and vicāra, wind is induced."
Wind also gives rise to karma.
It is free from the four conditions of desire;
its essence is exclusively wisdom.
It encompasses both the tainted and the untainted.
There are five conditions for falling away from the abandonment of desire.
Second, regarding those who newly cultivate wholesome factors:
One repeatedly contemplates the forms of men and women;
this involves three factors: the power of causes, the power of objects, and the power of improper mental attention.
This refers to one who practices in accordance with the dharmas that lead to decline.
These are the five factors of decline.
Regarding the textual passage on the severance of the roots of goodness, there are two parts;
the first clarifies the number of conditions.
Subsequently, regarding the distinctions between the manifest and the seeds in terms of abandonment,
there are either five conditions or six conditions.
First, those of sharp faculties.
Second, having evil intentions;
third, encountering evil friends;
fourth, heavy wrong views.
Fifth, they have no fear of evil.

Sixth, because they lack compassion for sentient beings, those of sharp faculties internally contemplate with such fierce and sharp wrong views that they do not fear any evils and fail to give rise to loving-kindness; thus, they sever their roots of goodness.
This is called severing the roots of goodness through the power of causes;
that is, by means of five conditions.
Furthermore, if one encounters evil friends who follow after evil inclinations and sever the roots of goodness—
This is called the severance of the roots of goodness through the power of conditions;
it possesses six conditions.
It must be severed by those of sharp faculties, not by those of dull faculties.
A broad and evil intention can sever [the roots of merit], whereas a narrow intention cannot.
This applies to humans in the three continents, excluding the northern continent (*uttarakuru*).
As stated in the *Abhidharmapada*: "The first [root]..."
Only the highest-grade (adhimātra-adhimātra) wrong view within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is capable of severing the roots of goodness, and no other; furthermore,
it is only the lower-grade wrong view regarding suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), not regarding cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*),
though some maintain it may apply to the lower-grade wrong views concerning all four truths.
The characteristic of universal pervasion belongs to none other than those who lack shame and dread;
it does not belong to the other two natures, as they do not fear evil.
Because one lacks compassion and,
by the power of these causes, severs the roots of goodness;
as for the power of conditions, it necessarily arises from associating with evil friends.
Regarding the *ātyantika* (one who is ultimately [incapable of liberation]) and the *icchantika* who possesses the lineage (*gotra*),
the Abhidharma treatises state that both sever their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) simultaneously.
There are two kinds of roots of goodness: first, seeds;
second, active manifestations.
To bend the power of the seeds so that they do not tend toward manifestation is called "abandonment";
it does not mean abandoning the seeds themselves.
This refers exclusively to abandoning the innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) of the desire realm, which are not produced through application (*prāyogika*).
Because the preparatory application (*prayoga*) has already ceased at the time of the preceding stage of preparation (*pūrvaprayoga*),
the abandonment of the nine grades does not occur in a single moment.
It is intended that they be abandoned through uninterrupted succession (*ānantarya*), unlike the destruction [of afflictions] by the Path (*mārga*).
There are four conditions for the restoration of the roots of goodness:
first, possessing sharp faculties;
second, seeing one's relatives and friends practicing merit.
Third, by approaching virtuous persons and hearing [the teaching on] cause and effect;
fourth, because of the preceding conditions, doubt arises;
and by realizing certainty, one reconnects with the roots of goodness.
Master Jing’s commentary explains:
When one first hears another speak of the existence of cause and effect,
at that moment, the ear-consciousness and the simultaneous mental consciousness constitute the "sudden-cognition" (*śūl-er-xin*).
That which gives rise to hesitation is the mind of seeking;
because it is indeterminate (avyākṛta), it is not the affliction of doubt.
That which realizes certainty is a mind of certainty;
it is also indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and not the right view of virtue (*kuśala-samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the restoration of the roots of goodness:
this is the stage of both defilement and purity;
it is within a mind of right view that the roots of goodness are restored.
At the time when the roots of goodness are severed, their active manifestation is severed;
now, as they are resumed,
the seeds of goodness exist previously and cannot be said to be newly resumed.

If it is said that when hesitation arises as the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*), and immediately thereafter a mind of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) arises, this is called "realizing certainty" (*niścaya-pratilambha*) and "reconnecting the roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla-pratisaṃdhi*);
then, within the five types of minds, under which category is this affliction of doubt subsumed?
If it were in a state of mind that is already determined, it could not be called doubt.
If it occurs in a state of mind that is either defiled or pure, how could doubt arise only after a determined state of mind?
Because of this contradiction, one must rely on the previous explanation.
Unlike the Sarvāstivādins, who hold that the roots of goodness are reconnected through either doubt or right view,
Sthiramati provides two interpretations.
The initial interpretation was consistent with [the previous] view;
furthermore, it states:

"If one of sharp faculties, upon a sudden reflection, gives rise to doubt and subsequently attains certainty, thereby reconnecting the roots of goodness, this is called 'reconnection through the power of the cause' (*hetu-bala*)."

If one who possesses sharp faculties, having later encountered virtuous friends and heard the true Dharma, gives rise to doubt and subsequently realizes certainty, thereby reconnecting their roots of goodness, this is called "reconnection through the power of conditions.
According to the second interpretation:
This is identical to the Sarvāstivāda in that it avoids partial acceptance or rejection.
Master Bei stated:
"Because doubt arises, the seeds continue."
Because it has correctly realized certainty, it continues to manifest.
Now, this is explained:
when one first encounters an object at the time of hearing the True Dharma and so forth, it is called the *sateri* mind (the sudden or adventitious mind).
Next, one seeks out names and so forth, as well as their definitive [meanings], yet without having definitively known the referents they express;
then, upon reaching a state of defilement or purity, or by giving rise to doubt, one subsequently reconnects with the roots of goodness.
Alternatively, it is because one continues the roots of goodness through right view itself.
Thus, it is said that by giving rise to doubt as a cause, one realizes certainty and thereby restores the roots of goodness.
If one interprets it in this way:
This is further based on the Sarvāstivāda school.
Within this context, both the acquisition of birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*) and the wholesome roots of application (*prayoga-kuśala*) are included.
At the time when the roots of goodness are severed, the superior dharmas are extinguished first.
Therefore, when right abandonment is attained and subsequently resumed, it depends on internal and external conditions;
for this reason, these two types of goodness are not fixed.
Because the production of roots of goodness through the superior external condition of hearing the true Dharma includes both preparatory skillful means and the actual attainment;
for by merely reflecting on it oneself or seeing others practicing merit, one frequently achieves subsequent births and subsequently induces the preparatory skillful means.
Alternatively, when first reconnecting the roots of goodness, one may give rise only to those obtained by birth (*upapattilābhika*);
this is because those produced through effort (*prayoga*) are difficult to generate,
and since the superior [roots] have already been severed previously.
Therefore, it continues; it continues the wholesome [states] of the desire realm,
but not those of the two higher realms.
The sudden continuum is not gradual;
because the gradual arising of other categories makes it difficult to exhaust them completely, there are nine.
Because it continues to arise immediately [after ceasing], it is one;
where there is a severance, there must be a continuation, yet where there is a continuation, there is not necessarily a severance.
As stated in the seventeenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*:
Is it possible to continue the roots of goodness within this very life?
It is indeed possible, with the exception of those who have committed the acts of immediate retribution.
That person will certainly be about to pass away from hell.
"About to pass away" means at the point of death; or it may refer to the moment they are about to take birth there.
"About to take birth" refers to the state of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), wherein, upon seeing the signs of the future rebirth, they immediately reconnect with their roots of virtue.
It is further said:
"The power of conditions severs the roots of goodness;
at the time of birth in hell, the continuity of that severed force is weak."
The roots of goodness are severed through the power of the cause;
this occurs at the time of death in hell because the power of the cause is strong.
Furthermore, it is the corruption of intention (*āśaya*), not the corruption of application (*prayoga*), that severs the roots of goodness.
Such a person is able to reconnect [the roots of goodness] in the present life.
However, for one who has severed the roots of goodness through both [wrong views and lack of faith], it is only after the destruction of the body that they reconnect the roots of goodness—
whether their [wrong] views have been destroyed or not.
The meaning is likewise so.
From here below, death and birth are elucidated.
This major section is divided into two parts.
First, the internal division of death and birth is explained;
subsequently, the external division of formation and destruction is explained.
Within the former, death and birth are first explained.

The second fascicle later states: "In this way, through successive transmission among all classes of sentient beings," and so forth, clarifying that one attains the exhaustion of outflows by contemplating emptiness.
Within the preceding section, it first clarifies death and subsequently clarifies birth.
The section on death has three parts:
first, a general enumeration of the six types of death;
second, a detailed explanation according to their sequence.
Third, regarding the performance of wholesome and unwholesome deeds, there follows an explanation of various meanings.
In the initial passage, it says: "That is to say, death occurs because of the exhaustion of the lifespan.
This is a general explanation of the meaning of death.
"Do not inquire whether the time for death is right or wrong;
it is simply the relinquishing of the name that defines the limit of one's lifespan within those six [periods].
Master Ki (Kaiyuan) explains this as follows:
Regarding the first three [stages] of death, it is the death of one whose consciousness is not clearly manifest, occurring at the very moment the consciousness departs from the body.
Regarding the latter three stages of death, it is the death of one whose conscious mind has not yet departed from the body, occurring as they are about to die.
Within the second section of the detailed explanation:
One who dies when their lifespan is exhausted is one whose karmic life has come to an end;
this is called timely death.
The latter two are called untimely deaths.
Lack of food and clothing is called the exhaustion of merit;
dying by other causes or through injustice is called not avoiding the uneven.
The nine causes are synonymous with the nine conditions;
they are separately designated as two sets of nine.
Regarding the seventh [ignorance]: it is ignorance concerning whether something will bring one harm or benefit.
They enter water or throw themselves into fire, or die from falling into pits due to their folly; eighth,
they engage in unchaste conduct at improper times—
committing it when hungry, when full, while traveling far, or during illness— and thus die.
Ninth, those who engage in non-measured conduct and non-celibacy die because their passionate attachment is excessive.
The Abhidharma speaks of three types of death.
First, death occurs because the lifespan is exhausted.
For example, those born in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) have a maximum lifespan of one hundred years;
although their karma is not yet exhausted, they die because their life-force is spent.
Second, death occurs because merit is exhausted;
death occurs because one is addicted to meditative concentration while lacking food, clothing, or external conditions;
and death occurs because the three types of karma are exhausted.
Because the karma of the three times has been exhausted,
this treatise explains death solely in reliance upon present conditions and not upon past conditions.
Therefore, there is no death through the exhaustion of karma.
Among external conditions, that which is separate from oneself is called the "exhaustion of merit," while that which is conjoined with oneself is called "inequality."
The *Abhidharmapada* generally explains that the combination of the two conditions—past and present—is termed "merit";
thus, the two treatises differ.
This is according to the *Abhidharmakośa*.
One may understand this by formulating four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) based on the exhaustion of lifespan versus the non-exhaustion of merit, and so forth.
If one follows the Abhidharma (Abhidharmakośa):
First, regarding death by the exhaustion of the life-span (*āyus*) and death by the exhaustion of karma (*karman*), four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established.
As for "death by the exhaustion of the life-span, but not by the exhaustion of karma": [it refers to]...
As in the Mahāyāna, a single karma may extinguish many births. For example:
first, death due to the exhaustion of the life-span of one birth, yet the force of the karma has not yet been exhausted;
second, death due to the exhaustion of karma, rather than the exhaustion of the life-span.
For example, there may be a single karma that brings about a lifespan of exactly one hundred years;
once those hundred years are complete, because one encounters superior conditions, the life span is further extended,
and one dies without exhausting that extended life.
The third can be understood.
As for the fourth, those who do not die at all [of their natural span],
they belong to the class of those who meet with untimely death.
Next, the death through the exhaustion of merit is contrasted with the death through the exhaustion of lifespan, forming four permutations.
Regarding those who die through the exhaustion of merit:

Because of its vastness,
there may be those whose forms are curved, defiled, or turbid;
since the cavity is not straight, it is difficult to settle the embryo therein.
That place is foul and filthy, with turbid fluids;
it is unfit to be grasped as a basis for support.

There are those who naturally possess the great ancestral legacy of their clan,

Twenty-one: giving rise to perverted views toward one's parents;

From here below, the existence of birth (*upapatti-bhava*) is elucidated.
The text is divided into two parts;
first, the initial reliance of the link of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*) is explained.
In the second fascicle, at its beginning, the presence or absence of seeds is analyzed.
In the preceding section, there are two parts:
first, a general indication of the basis and support.
Second, as for the detailed explanation of their meanings below:
within the sequence of first posing questions and subsequently providing explanations, there are five parts.
The first clarifies the characteristics of the basis upon which they rely.
Second, the sense faculties arise in this sequential order.
Third, the bases of the sense faculties also arise sequentially, which is termed "attaining completion.
Fourth, consciousness relies upon form, sharing its security and peril.
Regarding the five [stages], first it relies upon the flesh-and-heart, and later it is discarded from this;
"that which is produced as a single mass of thick semen and blood" refers to the formation of a single mass from the combined semen and blood of the parents.
Within this, the arising of craving and afflictions at the final moment of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is called "inversion" (*viparyāsa*).
The final body of the intermediate state is termed the "condition for inversion.
Then, that single segment of insentient semen and blood perishes simultaneously with the intermediate state.
At that very same time, through the power of the seeds,

there arises a subtle root, along with the primary elements (mahābhūta) that constitute the root and other impure constituents of the sentient being— such as semen and blood— which, being of the same nature as the root, coalesce into a mass.
Regarding the statement that within this *kalala* there are the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*),
Jing’s interpretation of this passage is that it establishes the capacity of the formative causes (*kāraṇa*) to exist independently of their products (*kārya*).
Next, regarding the explanation of non-separation from the same location:
this text refers to the time of initial birth, when the four sense-faculties have not yet arisen,
yet the primary element of earth already exists.
Because the earth occupies its own location,
it is able to exist separately; likewise,
when the six sense bases arise, the four faculties have already been produced.
Thus, the faculties and the great elements interpenetrate one another;
just as the locations of many lamps do not differ,
this is called "occupying the same location without separation."
Master Bei said:
"Although the five characteristics are distinct, they are all produced by the single earth element;
since the body-faculty already exists together with the earth element, [the other elements are present]."
The second part states:
"In that same location, the four faculties have not yet arisen.
Therefore, this text says:
There is no contradiction in the meaning of "being distinct.
Although the earth element exists, it does not construct the four sense-faculties;
therefore, it is only metaphorically designated as a "constructor" (bhūta) with respect to its general category.
Later, Basibandhu stated:
"At first there are the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the sense organs,
as well as the secondary elements (upādāya-rūpa) that support those sense organs."

That is to say, the primary elements that constitute the body and the primary elements of the sensory objects that support the body constitute the primary elements of the other four sense organs and so forth;
they do not exist as something else that arises through mutual dependence.
This is because it is that which is derived [from the primary elements]. Otherwise, would there not then be only the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) without anything derived from them?
For all four primary elements in the desire realm are not separate from visible form, tangibility, and so forth.
Question: The text states that the primary elements (mahābhūta) arise together with the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) and their bases (āśraya).
What is the difference between the "basis" (āśraya) and the "locus" (adhiṣṭhāna)?
The commentary states:
If one speaks directly of the "basis," it refers to the four great elements that constitute the sense organs themselves;
if one speaks of the "locus of the basis," it refers to the physical location.
"Place" (āyatana) refers to the four objects that serve as the basis for the sense faculties;
this is stated because it is mentioned in a general sense.
